clinicalPearls: SLE is an autoimmune disease driven by overactive innate and adaptive immunity, with tissue injury mediated by autoantibodies and immune complexes; cutaneous, musculoskeletal, and renal systems are most often affected, followed by pulmonary, hematologic, cardiovascular, serosal, and CNS involvement (p.2827).

Roughly 90% of patients are women, most of childbearing age; in the US the highest prevalence is in Black women, then Hispanic, White, and Asian/Pacific Islander women, and non-White patients tend to have more severe disease (p.2827).
Autoantibodies can be detectable years before clinical diagnosis, so seropositivity helps attribute nonspecific constitutional symptoms to SLE (p.2827, p.2830).

ANA at a titer of at least 1:80 is the best screening test and is present in nearly all patients; repeatedly negative immunofluorescence ANA makes the diagnosis unlikely, though about 5% of patients are ANA-negative (p.2832).

Anti-dsDNA (present in ~40-60%, specificity ~75-99%) and anti-Sm (present in ~30%, highly specific) are the only ANA subtypes in the EULAR/ACR criteria; rising anti-dsDNA with falling C3/C4 signals active disease, especially impending nephritis (p.2832, p.2830).

Lupus arthritis is a nonerosive polyarthritis of wrists, MCP/PIP joints, and knees; periarticular ligament damage can cause reversible Jaccoud-like deformities, and overlap with rheumatoid arthritis is termed 'rhupus' (p.2829).

The classic malar 'butterfly' rash spares the nasolabial folds (distinguishing it from rosacea); subacute cutaneous lupus is photosensitive and linked to anti-Ro/SSA, while discoid lesions are the most common chronic cutaneous form (p.2829).

Nephritis occurs in about 35% of patients, may be asymptomatic, and warrants screening every 3 months with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio; biopsy is generally prompted by UPCr >0.5 or declining renal function (p.2830, p.2833).

Antiphospholipid antibodies are present in ~50% of patients and markedly raise risk of arterial/venous thrombosis, thrombocytopenia, recurrent fetal loss, Libman-Sacks endocarditis, and stroke (p.2830, p.2832).

Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies can cross the placenta and cause neonatal lupus (transient rash/lab abnormalities or, less commonly, congenital heart block); high-titer Ro warrants fetal echocardiography screening (p.2836).
Avascular (osteo)necrosis should be suspected when pain is out of proportion in a single hip, shoulder, or knee, particularly with prior corticosteroid use (p.2829).

Some patients are categorized as 'type 1 lupus' (classic immune-driven features such as nephritis, arthritis, vasculitis, generally steroid-responsive) versus 'type 2 lupus' (fatigue, diffuse pain, cognitive dysfunction/'brain fog', less responsive to immunosuppression) (p.2827-2828).
harrison.pathophysiology: SLE arises from multiple immunoregulatory defects in genetically predisposed individuals interacting with environmental triggers. There is a strong genetic component (24% vs 2% concordance in monozygotic vs dizygotic twins; >150 GWAS susceptibility loci), with the MHC the most common association and nearly half of loci tied to type 1 interferon production or signaling (e.g., TLR7, IRF5/7/8, STAT4); complement-cascade defects (C1q, C1r, C1s, C2, C4) impair clearance of apoptotic debris and immune complexes and underlie severe monogenic disease. Environmental contributors include UV light, crystalline silica, smoking, sex hormones, Epstein-Barr virus, and gut-microbiome-related increased intestinal permeability. Innate defects cause excess cellular debris (high neutrophil turnover and NETosis) that overwhelms macrophage/dendritic clearance, triggering nucleic-acid sensors and TLRs in plasmacytoid dendritic cells to produce type 1 interferon, which sensitizes the adaptive immune system. Loss of B- and T-cell tolerance (including expansion of age-associated B cells, T follicular/peripheral helper cell help, and defective regulatory T cells) drives production of pathogenic autoantibodies; autoantibody-nucleic acid immune complexes deposit in tissue, activate monocytes, and produce inflammation, repair, and eventually fibrosis after recurrent flares.

Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage or acute pneumonitis (life-threatening pulmonary involvement)
Severe neuropsychiatric disease: psychosis, seizures, transverse myelitis, stroke
Severe thrombocytopenia (<20,000-50,000/uL) with bleeding risk, or life-threatening hemolytic anemia
Atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome / thrombotic microangiopathy (hemolysis, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes, low ADAMTS13, high LDH)
Mesenteric vasculitis (risk of intestinal perforation, bleeding, ischemia)
Antiphospholipid syndrome with arterial/venous thrombosis or catastrophic APS
Pulmonary arterial hypertension or prior arterial thrombosis in pregnancy (highest maternal mortality risk)
New chest pain in a young patient given accelerated atherosclerosis and premature coronary disease
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis and survival vary widely by geographic region, race/ethnicity, and access to care and medications. Most patients have active disease despite therapy or recurrent flares; about 15% have relatively mild disease. Renal disease is a major determinant of outcome: roughly 20% of US patients with class IV lupus nephritis die or develop ESRD within 10 years, and non-White patients more often progress to ESRD. Accelerated atherosclerosis becomes a leading cause of death after about 5 years of disease, with elevated myocardial infarction and stroke rates driven by both traditional risk factors and lupus-specific factors (antiphospholipid antibodies, high disease activity, low C3, high glucocorticoid dose, elevated homocysteine/leptin). Glucocorticoids contribute to irreversible, dose-dependent organ damage (cataracts, osteoporotic fractures, avascular necrosis, diabetes) even at low doses; class V nephritis carries a better renal prognosis than class III/IV. Sustained low disease activity (LLDAS) for 2 or more years is associated with significantly less damage, and meta-analyses suggest an increased overall risk of cancer and cancer-related death.
pitfalls: Treating ANA positivity as diagnostic: ANA occurs at low titer in healthy people and in many other autoimmune diseases; diagnosis ultimately rests on clinical judgment, and classification criteria were designed for trial enrollment, not diagnosis.
Excluding SLE because ANA is negative: about 5% of patients are ANA-negative, where anti-Ro/SSA can support the diagnosis.
Missing asymptomatic lupus nephritis or cytopenias by not screening quarterly, since renal and hematologic disease can be present without symptoms.
Attributing acute pulmonary infiltrates to lupus pneumonitis when infection looks identical on imaging.
Ascribing psychosis or confusion to neuropsychiatric lupus without ruling out glucocorticoid-induced psychosis and infectious encephalitis.
Overlooking avascular necrosis as a cause of disproportionate single-joint pain in patients on corticosteroids.
Confusing drug-induced lupus (antihistone-positive, usually sparing kidney/brain, resolving after withdrawal) with idiopathic SLE.
Using estrogen-containing contraceptives or HRT in patients with antiphospholipid antibodies or active disease, increasing thromboembolism risk.
Using direct oral anticoagulants instead of warfarin for concomitant APS, or continuing teratogenic agents (mycophenolate, methotrexate, warfarin) in pregnancy.
harrison.severityClassification: Lupus nephritis is graded by the International Society of Nephrology/Renal Pathology Society (ISN/RPS) classes: I (mesangial deposits without hypercellularity), II (mesangial proliferative), III (focal proliferative glomerulonephritis), IV (diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis), and V (membranous), with III/IV +/- V combinations carrying the highest risk; class V (~20% of nephritis) more often presents with nephrotic syndrome but has a better prognosis than III/IV. Disease activity is quantified with the SLEDAI (and SLEDAI-2K), where low disease activity is a score of 0-4 and remission a score of 0 (with stable hydroxychloroquine/immunosuppressive use and prednisone equivalent 5 mg/day or less). Overall disease severity is also stratified clinically as mild (constitutional symptoms, mild arthritis, rash <=9% BSA, platelets 50-100, SLEDAI <=6), moderate (rheumatoid-like arthritis, rash 9-18% BSA, platelets 20-50, serositis, SLEDAI 7-12), and severe (major organ-threatening disease such as cerebritis, myelitis, pneumonitis, mesenteric vasculitis; platelets <20; TTP-like or hemophagocytic syndrome; rash >18% BSA; SLEDAI >12). Treat-to-target endpoints include LLDAS and DORIS remission, and trials use SRI, BICLA, and CLASI instruments.
management: Hydroxychloroquine as background therapy for essentially all patients to reduce flares and organ damage
Glucocorticoids for active disease, tapered to the lowest effective dose, with steroid-sparing immunosuppression
Immunosuppressants such as mycophenolate, azathioprine or cyclophosphamide for major organ involvement including lupus nephritis
Biologic therapy with belimumab, anifrolumab, or rituximab for refractory or severe disease
Photoprotection, cardiovascular risk reduction, bone protection, and vaccination given infection and accelerated atherosclerotic risk
Monitoring of disease activity with anti-dsDNA titres, complement levels and renal parameters to detect flares and impending nephritis
Antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy where antiphospholipid antibodies confer thrombotic risk, with pre-conception planning and pregnancy co-management
Multidisciplinary care spanning rheumatology, nephrology and obstetrics as needed

valueTables.title: Diagnostic criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus

cells.text: Fixed erythema, flat or raised, over the malar eminences.
Erythematous circular raised patches with adherent keratotic scaling and follicular plugging; atrophic scarring may occur.
Rash after exposure to ultraviolet light.
Oral or nasopharyngeal ulcers observed by a physician.
Nonerosive arthritis of two or more peripheral joints with tenderness, swelling, or effusion.
Pleuritis or pericarditis documented by ECG, rub, or evidence of effusion.
Proteinuria above 0.5 g/d, or a urine dipstick grade (printed value unreadable), or cellular casts.
Seizures or psychosis without other cause.
Hemolytic anemia, or leukopenia (below 4000/uL), or lymphopenia (below 1500/uL), or thrombocytopenia (below 100,000/uL), in the absence of offending drugs.
Abnormal ANA titer by immunofluorescence or equivalent assay at any time, without drugs known to induce ANA.

valueTables.footnote: If 4 or more of these criteria are well documented at any time in a patient's history, SLE is likely. Specificity is about 95%; sensitivity is about 75%.
